title: Detroit Could Block Billionaire-Owned Concrete Plant From Further Neighborhood Expansion
author: Jena Brooker
content:
After years of community opposition, Detroit city officials have taken steps
to stop a concrete mixing facility from further expanding into a residential
neighborhood.

City Council members, acting on a recommendation last week from planning
officials, will soon consider a rezoning measure that would restrict
industrial activity at the site of the Kronos concrete plant and surrounding
area. The concrete facility at its current size could stay and continue to
operate as normal.

The planning recommendation comes after a [BridgeDetroit and ProPublica
investigation](https://www.propublica.org/article/detroit-kronos-morouns-
concrete-neighborhood-takeover) this year revealed how city officials helped
Crown Enterprises, a real estate company owned by Detroit’s wealthy Moroun
family, obtain property in Cadillac Heights and then provided latitude when
its Kronos facility violated environmental laws. Residents have been filing
complaints and protesting Kronos for years, frustrated by the dust, noise and
other issues created by the concrete operation.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2027/04/20250812-Maney-
Detroit-Concrete-016_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**Left in the Dust: How a Billionaire-Owned Concrete Plant Took Over a Detroit
Community** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/detroit-kronos-morouns-
concrete-neighborhood-takeover)

The City Planning Commission voted Oct. 22 to recommend a change to some of
the zoning in the neighborhood from heavy to light industrial, which allows
buildings such as warehouses but excludes facilities like concrete plants. The
commission also recommended that other lots be zoned for residential and
commercial purposes. Earlier this month, the commissioners unanimously voted
to exclude industrial zoning in the area adjacent to Kronos, but they stepped
back from that last week.

Crown has objected to any zoning change.

Sharon Buttry, who helped organize residents to protest against the Kronos
plant, said she is  glad the lots would be rezoned but was disappointed that
the earlier recommendation, which was more pedestrian- and transit-friendly,
didn’t stand.

Buttry said she fears that the latest zoning recommendation would make it
easier for Crown to expand eventually. “We still want them to shut down or
move,” she said.

The zoning plan was revisited at the request of City Planning Commissioner
Fred Russell Jr., who said the adjustment would create a buffer between
residents and the existing concrete plant.

The City Council, which will ultimately decide on the rezoning, has scheduled
a public hearing for Nov. 19.

Over the last seven years, Crown has obtained dozens of parcels in Cadillac
Heights — some through [a land deal with the city in
2019](https://www.bridgedetroit.com/one-of-detroits-most-powerful-families-is-
displacing-east-side-residents/) and others after residents sold their parcels
and left. In all, the company now owns more than 160 lots in the neighborhood,
most of which are barren.

### How a 2019 Land-Swap Deal Accelerated the Morouns’ Foothold

The Moroun family spent decades, from 1966 to 2018, records show, gradually
acquiring lots in Cadillac Heights through their various companies, eventually
putting the parcels all under the ownership of Crown Enterprises. A May 2019
deal with the city of Detroit allowed Crown to acquire dozens of additional
parcels during the next seven years.

![A map showing parcels owned by the Moroun family, through its Crown
Enterprises subsidiary, in a section of the Cadillac Heights neighborhood in
northeast Detroit. Parcels are colored based on the Moroun family’s  ownership
of more than 80 by 2019, when the land-swap deal with the city occurred, and
167 parcels as of June.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2300-detroit-concrete-parcels-impact.jpg)Note: Sale
dates for 19 parcels could not be identified, but records show Crown owned
them as of June. Sources: City of Detroit, Detroit’s Office of the Assessor,
Wayne County Register of Deeds, Detroit City Council. Chris
Alcantara/ProPublica

In a letter to Detroit officials in mid-September and Oct. 22, a law firm
representing Crown threatened legal action if city officials change the
zoning, arguing that doing so would devalue the property and create
uncertainty about future development.

Attorney Melvin Butch Hollowell also said if the rezoning goes through, the
city would be backtracking on its commitment to support Crown’s development in
Cadillac Heights. Crown obtained the land there in exchange for the company
swapping property in another part of the city, which allowed automaker
Stellantis to open [the first new car plant in Detroit in three
decades](https://www.degc.org/post/fca-investment-could-lead-to-5-000-new-
jobs-for-detroit).

City officials have said they didn’t know Crown’s plans included a concrete
facility. Crown did not present a specific plan at the time of the land
transfer. But after the concrete plant opened, the city in 2022 signed a
first-of-its-kind agreement with Crown that gave the company time to fix
issues before being penalized. The agreement has allowed the company to avoid
fines on several occasions, the news organizations have documented.

In response to questions from BridgeDetroit and ProPublica, a Crown
spokesperson said the company has invested more than $10 million to develop
the concrete operation based “on the City’s promises and actions of approving
our plans for this facility.”

“The property was traded to us for the express purpose of redevelopment,” the
spokesperson, Kenneth Dobson, wrote.

Dobson said that if the zoning changes, the company will not make the
improvements it has promised, including new landscaping and sidewalks. He
claimed the improvements would not be allowed under the new zoning and that
they also wouldn’t be a sound business decision. City planning staff, however,
said the company can still make the improvements.

The neighborhood surrounding Kronos has been zoned to allow heavy industry
since the 1940s, when a rail line operated there. Before the concrete
operation, the land was occupied by a trucking depot for decades.

Despite the zoning designation, the neighborhood attracted working-class
families who lived in modest single-family houses. Buddy’s Pizza, famous as
the birthplace of Detroit-style pizza, was founded there and drew crowds from
across the city.

The City Planning Commission’s votes this month were four years in the making
and part of a broader evaluation of land near the proposed Joe Louis Greenway,
a walking and biking trail that will traverse the city and is already under
construction.

Scott Benson, the council member who represents Cadillac Heights, asked the
planning commission in 2023 to consider whether the industrial zoned areas
along the greenway should be rezoned to a use that better supports safety and
public health. He said the request at first was unrelated to Kronos, but then
[community input further influenced the desire for
change](https://www.bridgedetroit.com/detroit-looks-to-rezone-parcels-along-
the-joe-louis-greenway/).

“That did play a role here,” he said in an interview. “The community came out
and said, ‘Yes, we especially want this part done and it abuts the Joe Louis
Greenway.’”

![A man wearing a suit holds his chin in his hands while he sits in a
government building. In front of him is a placard that reads, “Council Member
Benson,” and behind him is an American flag.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260224-Hagen-
DetroitConcrete-1079_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Scott Benson
represents Cadillac Heights in the Detroit City Council. Nick Hagen for
ProPublica

More than 30 people — some in favor of a zoning change and some against —
spoke out at recent commission meetings. Kronos employees and others told the
commission that the company has created jobs for Detroit residents and said
Crown has invested in the neighborhood with new paving.

Terrell Daniel, whom the city identified in meeting minutes as a Kronos
employee, urged the commission at its Oct. 1 meeting to continue to allow
industry in the neighborhood.

“It’s bringing back the backbone of Detroit,” he said. He said the concrete
plant has provided an opportunity “for guys who never had a chance to work in
the city.”

Those in support of rezoning expressed concerns about the dust, air quality
and Crown’s track record of not taking care of the neighborhood, which has
included leaving vacant homes unsecured and messy.

![A dilapidated house with no front windows and an overgrown, trash-covered
lawn.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20260623-Hagen-
DetroitConcrete-0442_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)A house that
Crown purchased in January has no front door or first-floor windows, and trash
litters the yard. Nick Hagen for ProPublica

Residents have filed about 80 complaints to both city and state environmental
offices, according to records obtained by BridgeDetroit and ProPublica. They
have described “literal whiteout conditions” and “dust clouds” that blanket
their neighborhood and irritate their eyes.

The city has issued several tickets to Kronos for violating Detroit’s
[fugitive dust ordinance](https://detroitmi.gov/departments/buildings-safety-
engineering-and-environmental-department-bseed/bseed-divisions/environmental-
affairs/fugitive-dust-ordinance), passed in 2024 to limit pollution. The law
requires businesses such as concrete plants and scrapyards to submit plans to
limit dust and prevent it from spreading into neighborhoods.

On Oct. 7, the city received a complaint about Kronos and an inspector found
the company had spread dust in the neighborhood and had piles of materials
that should have been blocked from view, according to city spokesperson
Georgette Johnson.

Kronos wrote in a letter to the city that it swept and watered the streets and
reduced the height of the piles. Johnson said Crown corrected the problems.

Dobson said readings from its air monitors have never exceeded the city’s
pollution limits and that a small number of people regularly complain. He
previously said that the company planned to demolish a vacant home littered
with trash but was waiting on utilities to be disconnected.
